steps.title: Both directions at once
steps.body: Put the pieces together: neurons signal to immune cells (neuropeptides, B6) and immune cells signal to neurons (cytokines, B7). It's a genuine loop — each can trigger the other, and the loop can amplify or settle an inflammatory state.

steps.prompt: Match each direction to its typical messenger.
steps.explanation: Neurons mostly use neuropeptides to reach immune cells; immune cells mostly use cytokines to reach neurons.

steps.setup: Neurons release CGRP that recruits immune activity, and the resulting cytokines further sensitize the neurons.
steps.prompt: What kind of dynamic is this?
options: Positive feedback that can amplify inflammation
A one-way signal from neurons to immune cells
Negative feedback that settles the response
Two parallel responses to the same trigger
steps.reveal: Each side drives the other, so the loop can run away (amplify) — one reason chronic neuroinflammatory conditions are self-sustaining. Breaking the loop at either limb is a therapeutic strategy.

variants.prompt: Neurons exciting immunity, which then sensitizes the neurons, is…
variants.explanation: Mutual activation makes a positive feedback loop.

sources.citation: Wallrapp A & Chiu IM, 2024, Annu Rev Immunol
sources.note: Review of bidirectional neuroimmune interactions in the intestine.
